abstract: Pervasive transcription generates diverse RNAs, including promoter-upstream transcripts (PROMPTs), coding and non-coding transcripts from protein-coding loci, and enhancer RNAs. How their full-length architectures relate to RNA fate remains poorly understood. Using ultra-deep sequencing of polyadenylated and non-polyadenylated capped RNAs from mouse embryonic stem cells, we show that nuclear exosome surveillance of PROMPTs is associated with transcript length and sequence composition. We show that for most protein-coding genes, capped transcripts are dominated by cytosolic 3'[->]5' degradation intermediates or premature transcription termination products rather than full-length mRNAs. The relative abundance of intact mRNAs, cytosolic degradation intermediates and prematurely terminated transcripts varies between genes and is associated with gene architecture, expression level and biological function. Finally, we identify a class of convergently transcribed enhancers enriched for Polycomb repressive complex 2-associated proteins and poised enhancer features, with an increased propensity for activation during differentiation. Full-length transcript architecture thus reveals RNA fate and regulatory state.
